content.thinking:
This one hits the competence dimension of trust by addressing the classic "models can't predict" skepticism, backed by a credible Science magazine source with concrete numeric track records. It's a bit dry but the acknowledgment of limitations adds integrity, so I'd expect around +2.3 on multidimensional trust.

I'm working through the secondary outcomes: trust_post around +1.6, distrust down around -1.3, modest funding bump near +0.8, policy_role and inst_trust more diluted around +0.7-0.9. Belief in human-caused warming gets a decent lift near +1.0 since the piece ties prediction accuracy to pollution as the driver, with smaller downstream effects on concern (+0.8), general policy support (+0.6), specific policies (+0.5), behavior (+0.3), and tiny bumps to AMS donation (~+0.08) and newsletter signup (~+0.008). I'm settling on decisive non-round values for each.

content.text: {"reasoning_summary": "This arm directly rebuts a concrete, widely circulated skeptic criticism ('models can't predict the future') with a verifiable 50-year track record from a high-credibility source (Science), which loads squarely on the competence dimension of the multidimensional trust battery; the candid acknowledgment of where models erred (and why — human-emissions inputs, not physics) should also nudge integrity/openness perceptions rather than raising suspicion. It is counter-attitudinal evidence for skeptics, but the format is dry and expository rather than narrative or messenger-based, and there is no interactive correction, so I place it slightly above the average arm on the primary trust outcome (~+2.2, d≈0.09) but not at the top. Because accuracy of prediction implies the warming signal and its anthropogenic input are real, belief and concern get modest positive spillover (~+1), attenuated further by pre-treatment anchoring on the re-asked belief/trust single items. Funding perceptions and scientists' policy role get small positive effects (demonstrated competence justifies both), while institutional trust is diluted by the federal-government item.
